topic: Maximum likelihood estimation: likelihood as a function of parameters
audience: Undergraduate economics students (ECON 167 / similar); calculus-based probability; first encounter with likelihood as a function of parameters
learningOutcomes: Write the likelihood of an i.i.d. sample as a function of a parameter and distinguish it from the probability of data given a known parameter.
Sketch why maximizing the likelihood (or log-likelihood) is a method of point estimation, using a one-parameter example (e.g. Bernoulli or Normal mean).
Explain in the course's own analogy (from lecture notes) what the MLE is doing, without substituting a grade-school 'likely/unlikely' vocabulary.
State one limitation of MLE that the course actually teaches (regularity, invariance, or finite-sample behavior) as given in the notes — mark unknown if the notes do not say.

sections.title: Hook: the lecture analogy, not a weather forecast
sections.purpose: Activate the course's own MLE analogy from notes and block grade-school likelihood language from taking over.

sections.title: Likelihood as a function of the parameter
sections.purpose: Write L(theta | data) for an i.i.d. sample and contrast it with P(data | theta known).

sections.title: Why we maximize (log) likelihood
sections.purpose: Treat MLE as a point estimator on a one-parameter example the course actually uses.

sections.title: One limitation as the notes state it
sections.purpose: Record a course-true caveat or explicitly mark unknown if the uploaded notes do not say.

sections.title: Individual check
sections.purpose: Each student writes L(theta) for a tiny sample and one sentence on what maximizing it is doing; chatting with notes is not this check.
